newsitem.title: HAITI: Attention turns to Aristide as Haiti gov't crumbles.
newsitem.headline: Attention turns to Aristide as Haiti gov't crumbles.

text.p: As Haiti's political system tumbles around President Rene Preval with the postponement of Sunday's run-off elections and threatened boycotts, his predecessor Jean-Bertrand Aristide was moving back to centre stage.

In another blow, Prime Minister Rosny Smarth resigned last Monday as head of the government after pressure from many sectors that he was incapable of completing the immense task of bettering the lives of Haiti's poor.
Aristide, in a broadcast after the resignation, criticised the government's U.S.-backed economic programme, which includes privitizing nine state-run industries.
"It is a game of organising their own business rules which are good for those that have more, and bad for those that have less," Aristide said.
The U.S. State Department on Tuesday issued a statement that analysts interpreted as a call for Aristide to back off.
"We think President Preval ought to be given the opportunity and the political space to govern. It is very difficult to succeed someone as popular as Aristide," it said.
Critics have accused Aristide of provoking violence by grassroots organisations that had demanded Smarth's resignation. Aristide has denied involvement in violence.

Last month Aristide's former friend Paul Dejean, the Minister of Haitians Living Abroad, reportedly said Aristide had an "immense ambition for power," and he was responisble for the tension, insecurity and disorder in the capital.

Enrique Ter Horst, in charge of the United Nations mission in Haiti, said: "There is a lot of speculation on who is behind the violence." When asked at whom the fingers were pointing he replied: "The direction you know."
Danny Toussaint, a member of Aristide's Fanmi Lavalas party, refuted the accusations and blamed the United States for stirring things up.

"There is a plot against Aristide. The U.S. offered me a job, money and a car if I would say it was Aristide that was causing all the disaster in Haiti," he said at a news conference on Wednesday, responding to the American statement.
Toussaint is a former Haitian army captain who defected from the military in 1986 and became Aristide's head of security during his 1990 presidential campaign.

Aristide, who rose to power on a popular revolution that ousted the Duvalier family's 30-year dictatorship in 1986, was elected president in 1990. Seven months later he was driven into exile by a military coup. He finished his five-year term after being restored to power in October 1994, by a U.S.-led military intervention.
On Feb. 7, 1996, the first democratic transfer of power in Haiti's history took place between Aristide and his annointed successor Preval.

But Aristide sniped from the sidelines at government plans and eventually split from the ruling Lavalas Political Organisation to form his own party, the Fanmi Lavalas, who follow an anti-privatisation stance.
Discontent simmered as the government failed to alleviate hardship and misery in the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere.

Elections for nine senatorial seats and local councils were held on April 6 and were seen as crucial for the implementation of the government's economic plan, which was backed by the International Monetary Fund, World Bank and foreign donors.

Fanmi Lavalas dominated the first round but Sunday's scheduled run-off elections for seven seats were postponed for a second time due to pressure from the international community and the Lavalas Political Organisation.
Most of the parties from the first round said they would boycott the second due to irregularities. They claimed the Provisional Electoral Council tried to manipulate results.
The United States said postponing the second-round balloting was a "rational step" that would strengthen the electoral process, provided a firm date was set to hold them.

"This will allow sufficient time for the (electoral) council to implement measures which will enhance the integrity and transparency of the electoral process," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Friday.
Washington has emphasised it wants the Haitian government to continue with the economic direction Smarth took.
